# stopcock

> Fast, composable TypeScript packages for functional programming, dates, async work, HTTP, state, diffing, linear algebra, automatic differentiation, signal processing, color, SVG, and image processing.

Packages are independently installable under the `@stopcock` scope.

## Install

```bash
bun add @stopcock/fp
```

---
# Algebra and ordering

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/algebra/

Eq, Hash, Ord, Semigroup, Monoid, Group, and Ordering

The algebra modules are small plain objects and functions. They do not require
classes, higher-kinded-type emulation, or a runtime typeclass registry.

```ts
import * as Eq from '@stopcock/fp/eq'
import * as Hash from '@stopcock/fp/hash'
import * as Ord from '@stopcock/fp/ord'
import * as Semigroup from '@stopcock/fp/semigroup'
import * as Monoid from '@stopcock/fp/monoid'
import * as Group from '@stopcock/fp/group'
```

## Equality

```ts
const pointEq = Eq.struct<Point>({
  x: Eq.number,
  y: Eq.number,
})

pointEq.equals({ x: 1, y: 2 }, { x: 1, y: 2 }) // true
```

`Eq.deep` is cycle-safe for dense arrays and plain records. Dates, maps, sets,
regular expressions, promises, and class instances are atomic unless you
provide a domain-specific instance.

## Hashing

Hash instances provide deterministic integer hashes and compose over common
containers:

```ts
const pointHash = Hash.struct<Point>({
  x: Hash.number,
  y: Hash.number,
})
```

Use compatible `Eq` and `Hash` instances whenever a hashed collection relies on
both.

## Ordering

```ts
const byAge = Ord.contramap((user: User) => user.age)(Ord.number)
const byAgeThenName = Ord.combine(byAge, Ord.contramap((user: User) => user.name)(Ord.string))

users.toSorted(byAgeThenName.compare)
```

The `ordering` module contains the `-1 | 0 | 1` primitives used by `Ord`.

## Combining values

```ts
const total = Semigroup.numberSum.combine(2, 3)
const all = Monoid.booleanAll.combineAll([true, true, false])
const delta = Group.numberSum.subtract(10, 3)
```

- A `Semigroup<A>` combines two `A` values.
- A `Monoid<A>` adds an identity value and folds empty collections.
- A `Group<A>` adds inversion/removal.

Instances are ordinary values, so application-specific instances are easy to
create and test.

---
# A (Array)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/array/

Filter, map, sort, group, and 30+ array functions for pipe

Every function works both ways: `A.fn(arr, ...)` (data-first) and `pipe(arr, A.fn(...))` (data-last). Streaming operations such as `map`, `filter`, `flatMap`, `take`, `drop`, `takeWhile`, and `dropWhile` [fuse in pipe](/concepts/fusion) into single loops. Terminal folds, accessor terminals, and materializing operations have different boundaries.

## Accessors

```ts
head<A>(arr: readonly A[]): Option<A>
last<A>(arr: readonly A[]): Option<A>
first<A>(arr: readonly A[]): Option<A> // alias for head
headOrUndefined<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A | undefined
lastOrUndefined<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A | undefined
headNonEmpty<A>(arr: readonly [A, ...A[]]): A
lastNonEmpty<A>(arr: readonly [A, ...A[]]): A
tail<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A[]           // all except first
init<A>(arr: readonly A[]): A[]           // all except last
length<A>(arr: A[]): number
isEmpty<A>(arr: A[]): boolean
```

`head`, `last`, `length`, and `isEmpty` are accessor terminals in fused chains.
Option-returning names are the default; `*OrUndefined` is the explicit
JavaScript interop escape hatch.

## Transforms

```ts
map<A, B>(arr: A[], f: (a: A) => B): B[]
mapWithIndex<A, B>(arr: A[], f: (a: A, i: number) => B): B[]
filter<A>(arr: A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): A[]
filterWithIndex<A>(arr: A[], pred: (a: A, i: number) => boolean): A[]
flatMap<A, B>(arr: A[], f: (a: A) => B[]): B[]
reduce<A, B>(arr: A[], f: (acc: B, a: A) => B, init: B): B
reduceRight<A, B>(arr: A[], f: (acc: B, a: A) => B, init: B): B
scan<A, B>(arr: A[], f: (acc: B, a: A) => B, init: B): B[]
forEach<A>(arr: A[], f: (a: A) => void): void
forEachWithIndex<A>(arr: A[], f: (a: A, i: number) => void): void
```

`map`, `mapWithIndex`, `filter`, `filterWithIndex`, and `flatMap` stream in fused `pipe` chains. `reduce` is a terminal fold. `forEach` is terminal side-effect traversal. `scan` returns an intermediate array.

## Ordering

```ts
sort(arr: number[]): number[]
sortBy<A>(arr: A[], cmp: (a: A, b: A) => number): A[]
reverse<A>(arr: A[]): A[]
```

Materialization boundaries. They need the whole array. When callback purity is
explicitly promised, `compilePure` can apply its bounded stable top-k rewrite
to an adjacent `sortBy -> take(k)` or `sort -> take(k)` pair; ordinary `pipe`
and `compile` keep exact semantics.

## Slicing

```ts
take<A>(arr: A[], n: number): A[]
drop<A>(arr: A[], n: number): A[]
takeWhile<A>(arr: A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): A[]
dropWhile<A>(arr: A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): A[]
chunk<A>(arr: A[], n: number): A[][]
slidingWindow<A>(arr: A[], n: number): A[][]
aperture<A>(arr: A[], n: number): A[][]
```

`take`, `drop`, `takeWhile`, and `dropWhile` can stream in fused pipelines. `take` and `takeWhile` can stop early.

## Search

```ts
find<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): Option<A>
findIndex<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): Option<number>
findOrUndefined<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): A | undefined
findIndexOrUndefined<A>(arr: readonly A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): number | undefined
every<A>(arr: A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): boolean
some<A>(arr: A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): boolean
includes<A>(arr: A[], value: A): boolean
```

`find`, `every`, and `some` are terminal predicates/searches. They can run as the final step of a fused pass and bail out early.

## Deduplication

```ts
uniq<A>(arr: A[]): A[]
uniqBy<A, B>(arr: A[], f: (a: A) => B): A[]
```

Deduplication needs seen-value state and returns a materialized array.

## Set operations

```ts
intersection<A>(a: A[], b: A[]): A[]
union<A>(a: A[], b: A[]): A[]
difference<A>(a: A[], b: A[]): A[]
symmetricDifference<A>(a: A[], b: A[]): A[]
```

## Combinators

```ts
zip<A, B>(a: A[], b: B[]): [A, B][]
zipWith<A, B, C>(a: A[], b: B[], f: (a: A, b: B) => C): C[]
xprod<A, B>(a: A[], b: B[]): [A, B][]
groupBy<A>(arr: readonly A[], f: (a: A) => string): Record<string, A[]>
partition<A>(arr: A[], pred: (a: A) => boolean): [A[], A[]]
intersperse<A>(arr: A[], sep: A): A[]
flatten<A>(arr: A[][]): A[]
transpose<A>(arr: A[][]): A[][]
```

`groupBy` is a materialization boundary because it needs the whole grouped result.

## Mutation (immutable)

```ts
adjust<A>(arr: A[], index: number, f: (a: A) => A): A[]
update<A>(arr: A[], index: number, value: A): A[]
insert<A>(arr: A[], index: number, value: A): A[]
remove<A>(arr: A[], index: number, count: number): A[]
```

All return new arrays.

## Constructors

```ts
range(start: number, end: number): number[]
repeat<A>(value: A, n: number): A[]
times<A>(f: (i: number) => A, n: number): A[]
unfold<A, B>(f: (seed: B) => [A, B] | undefined, seed: B): A[]
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'

type Product = {
  name: string
  price: number
  category: string
  inStock: boolean
}

// fused: filter -> map -> take runs in one loop
const deals = pipe(
  products,
  A.filter((p: Product) => p.inStock && p.price < 50),
  A.map((p) => ({ name: p.name, price: p.price })),
  A.take(10),
)

// group + count
const byCategory = A.groupBy(products, (p) => p.category)
// { electronics: [...], clothing: [...] }

// rolling total
A.scan([100, 200, 150, 300], (acc, x) => acc + x, 0)
// [100, 300, 450, 750]

// remove duplicates by key
const uniqueCustomers = pipe(
  orders,
  A.uniqBy((o: { customerId: string }) => o.customerId),
)

// set operations
const newUsers = A.difference(allUsers, existingUsers)
const commonTags = A.intersection(tagsA, tagsB)

// batch processing
const batches = A.chunk(records, 100)
```

---
# B (Boolean)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/boolean/

not, and, or, ifElse. Boolean combinators for pipe

```ts
not_(a: boolean): boolean
and_(a: boolean, b: boolean): boolean      // dual
or_(a: boolean, b: boolean): boolean       // dual
ifElse<A>(cond: boolean, onTrue: () => A, onFalse: () => A): A  // dual
```

Trailing underscores avoid colliding with JS reserved words.

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as B from '@stopcock/fp/boolean'

pipe(true, B.not_) // false
pipe(true, B.and_(false)) // false
pipe(
  false,
  B.ifElse(
    () => 'yes',
    () => 'no',
  ),
) // 'no'

// toggle a feature flag
const toggled = pipe(isEnabled, B.not_)

// both conditions must hold
const canAccess = pipe(isAdmin, B.and_(isActive))
```

---
# Dict migration

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/dict/

Dict was replaced by Record in @stopcock/fp 2.0

The 1.x `D` namespace and `/dict` subpath were removed. Use the property-key
aware record module:

```diff
- import { D } from '@stopcock/fp'
+ import * as Record from '@stopcock/fp/record'

- D.toEntries(values)
+ Record.entries(values)
```

The new module includes immutable `get`, `set`, `remove`, `modify`, `update`,
`map`, `filter`, `filterMap`, `mapKeys`, `merge`, `pick`, `omit`, `partition`,
`reduce`, and equality operations. Bulk construction and transforms have
explicit `fromEntriesInto`, `mapInto`, and `filterInto` forms.

Unlike the old string-only `Dict` vocabulary, records preserve enumerable
`PropertyKey` values, including symbols.

---
# G (Guards)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/guards/

isString, isNumber, isNil, isDeepEqual and more. Runtime type guards with TypeScript predicates

Runtime type checks that narrow the TypeScript type.

```ts
type Guard<A> = Refinement<unknown, A>
```

## Type checks

```ts
isString(x: unknown): x is string
isNumber(x: unknown): x is number
isFiniteNumber(x: unknown): x is number
isNonBlankString(x: unknown): x is string
isBoolean(x: unknown): x is boolean
isBigInt(x: unknown): x is bigint
isSymbol(x: unknown): x is symbol
isFunction(x: unknown): x is Function
isDate(x: unknown): x is Date
isError(x: unknown): x is Error
isPromise(x: unknown): x is Promise<unknown>
isArray(x: unknown): x is unknown[]
isObjectType(x: unknown): x is object
isPlainObject(x: unknown): x is Record<string, unknown>
isArrayOf<A>(guard: Guard<A>): Guard<A[]>
isRecordOf<A>(guard: Guard<A>): Guard<Record<string, A>>
```

`isPlainObject` rejects arrays and class instances. `isObjectType` is just a `typeof` check.
`isRecordOf` accepts only plain objects and checks every own enumerable string-keyed value. Empty
arrays and records are valid because every contained value satisfies the supplied guard.

## Nullability

```ts
isNil(x: unknown): x is null | undefined
isNotNil<T>(x: T | null | undefined): x is T
isNull(x: unknown): x is null
isUndefined(x: unknown): x is undefined
isNullish(x: unknown): x is null | undefined
isNonNull<T>(x: T | null): x is T
isNonNullish<T>(x: T | null | undefined): x is T
isDefined<T>(x: T | undefined): x is T
```

## Equality

```ts
isDeepEqual(a: unknown, b: unknown): boolean
isShallowEqual(a: unknown, b: unknown): boolean
isStrictEqual(a: unknown, b: unknown): boolean
```

## Other

```ts
isEmpty(x: unknown): boolean
isEmptyish(x: unknown): boolean        // null, undefined, or empty
isTruthy(x: unknown): boolean
is<T>(ctor: new (...args: any[]) => T, val: unknown): val is T
propIs<T>(ctor: new (...args: any[]) => T, prop: string, obj: Record<string, unknown>): boolean
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'
import * as G from '@stopcock/fp/guard'

// narrow unknown API data
const data: unknown[] = [1, 'hello', null, { a: 1 }]
data.filter(G.isNumber) // [1], typed as number[]
data.filter(G.isNonNullish) // [1, 'hello', { a: 1 }]

// validate form field
if (G.isString(input) && !G.isEmpty(input)) {
  submit(input)
}

// filter mixed arrays in pipe
pipe(
  rawValues,
  A.filter(G.isNumber), // unknown[] → number[]
  A.filter((n) => n > 0),
)

// deep equality check
G.isDeepEqual({ a: [1, 2] }, { a: [1, 2] }) // true

// check class instance
G.is(Date, new Date()) // true
G.is(Date, '2024-01-01') // false

const numbers = G.isArrayOf(G.isFiniteNumber)
numbers([1, 2, 3]) // true
numbers([1, Number.NaN]) // false

const labels = G.isRecordOf(G.isNonBlankString)
labels({ primary: 'Save', secondary: 'Cancel' }) // true
```

---
# Iter

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/iter/

Lazy synchronous sequences with correct iterator closing

```ts
import * as Iter from '@stopcock/fp/iter'
```

`Iter<A>` is a lazy `Iterable<A>`. Operators do no work until a terminal pulls
the sequence. Constructors in this module are repeatable; `Iter.from` reflects
the repeatability of the iterable you provide.

## Constructors

```ts
Iter.from(iterable)
Iter.fromIterator(() => iterator)
Iter.defer(() => iterable)
Iter.empty()
Iter.of(1, 2, 3)
Iter.range(0, 10, 2)
Iter.repeat(value)
Iter.iterate(seed, next)
Iter.unfold(seed, step)
```

`range` excludes its end. `repeat` and `iterate` are infinite; pair them with a
bounded terminal such as `take`.

## Transformations

The core lazy vocabulary includes:

```ts
Iter.map(f)
Iter.filter(predicate)
Iter.filterMap(f)
Iter.flatMap(f)
Iter.flatten
Iter.tap(effect)
Iter.take(count)
Iter.drop(count)
Iter.takeWhile(predicate)
Iter.dropWhile(predicate)
Iter.scan(reducer, initial)
Iter.chunk(size)
Iter.intersperse(separator)
Iter.distinct
Iter.distinctBy(key)
Iter.concat(other)
Iter.zip(other)
Iter.zipWith(other, combine)
```

Transformations are usable directly or in `pipe`:

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'

const result = pipe(
  Iter.range(1, Infinity),
  Iter.filter((value) => value % 2 === 0),
  Iter.map((value) => value * value),
  Iter.take(3),
  Iter.toArray,
)
// [4, 16, 36]
```

## Terminals

```ts
Iter.toArray(source)
Iter.toArrayInto(source, target)
Iter.reduce(source, reducer, initial)
Iter.forEach(source, effect)
Iter.first(source) // Option<A>
Iter.last(source)  // Option<A>
Iter.find(source, predicate) // Option<A>
Iter.some(source, predicate)
Iter.every(source, predicate)
Iter.count(source)
```

Partial terminals return `Option`; absence is never encoded as an ambiguous
`undefined`.

## Resource safety

Short-circuiting operations call `return()` on an upstream iterator when it is
still open. This matters for generators that own file handles, cursors, or
other resources:

```ts
function* rows() {
  try {
    yield* databaseCursor
  } finally {
    databaseCursor.close()
  }
}

Iter.toArray(Iter.take(rows(), 10))
```

The `finally` block runs after the tenth value.

---
# Lens migration

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/lenses/

The 2.0 optic module replaces the old root lens helpers

The 1.x root lens helpers were replaced by the unified
`@stopcock/fp/optic` module. Import the module explicitly:

```diff
- import { prop, view, set, over } from '@stopcock/fp'
+ import * as Optic from '@stopcock/fp/optic'

- const name = view(user, prop<User, 'name'>('name'))
+ const name = Optic.view(Optic.prop<User, 'name'>('name'), user)

- const updated = over(user, prop<User, 'name'>('name'), String.toUpperCase)
+ const updated = Optic.modify(
+   Optic.prop<User, 'name'>('name'),
+   user,
+   String.toUpperCase,
+ )
```

The new module covers lenses, optionals, prisms, traversals, isomorphisms,
getters, folds, setters, keyed `At` optics, composition, a fluent builder, and
law helpers. Read the [Optic API](/api/optic).

---
# Logic migration

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/logic/

Logic was split into focused function and guard modules

The broad 1.x `Logic` namespace was removed from the 2.0 public surface.

Use `@stopcock/fp/function` for function-level composition:

```ts
import * as Fn from '@stopcock/fp/function'

Fn.complement(predicate)
Fn.ifElse(predicate, onTrue, onFalse)
Fn.always(value)
```

Use `@stopcock/fp/guard` for predicate and refinement composition:

```ts
import * as G from '@stopcock/fp/guard'

const nonBlank = G.and(G.isString, G.isNonBlankString)
const stringOrNumber = G.or(G.isString, G.isNumber)
const notNullish = G.not(G.isNullish)
```

Use `@stopcock/fp/eq` for domain equality, `@stopcock/fp/match` for lightweight
tagged-data dispatch, or the full `@stopcock/pattern` companion for structural
and exhaustive pattern matching.

---
# M (Math)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/math/

add, multiply, sum, mean, median. Arithmetic and stats for pipe

## Non-dual

```ts
inc(n: number): number
dec(n: number): number
negate(n: number): number
product(arr: number[]): number
```

## Dual

```ts
add(a: number, b: number): number
subtract(a: number, b: number): number
multiply(a: number, b: number): number
divide(a: number, b: number): number
modulo(a: number, b: number): number
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'
import * as M from '@stopcock/fp/math'

// apply discount
pipe(prices, A.map(M.multiply(0.9))) // 10% off

// offset scores
pipe(rawScores, A.map(M.add(curve)))

// compound product
M.product([2, 3, 4]) // 24

// counter operations
pipe(count, M.inc) // count + 1
pipe(count, M.dec) // count - 1
pipe(value, M.negate) // -value

// data-first
M.modulo(17, 5) // 2
```

# Module catalogue

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/modules/

Every public @stopcock/fp 2.0 entrypoint

`@stopcock/fp` keeps its root small. Import specialist APIs from these stable,
tree-shakeable subpaths.

## Collections and sequences

| Subpath | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `/array` | Eager array operators, fused pipeline steps, explicit `*Into` writes |
| `/readonly-array` | Read-only alias of the array vocabulary |
| `/non-empty-array` | Constructors and total operations for non-empty arrays |
| `/tuple` | Typed tuple construction, mapping, zipping, and projection |
| `/record` | Immutable property-keyed record operations |
| `/map` | Immutable `Map` operations |
| `/set` | Immutable `Set` operations |
| `/typed-array` | Numeric typed-array transforms and explicit destination buffers |
| `/indexed` | Shared indexed-collection operations |
| [`/iter`](/api/iter) | Lazy synchronous sequences |
| `/transducer` | Composable allocation-free reducing transformations |
| `/collector` | Reusable terminal collectors |

## Data and errors

| Subpath | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| [`/option`](/api/option) | Explicit absence |
| [`/result`](/api/result) | Fail-fast recoverable errors |
| [`/validation`](/api/validation) | Accumulating independent errors |
| [`/schema`](/api/schema) | Standard Schema V1 production and consumption |
| `/these` | Left, right, or both values |
| `/nullable` | Focused nullable boundary helpers |

Asynchronous failures and asynchronous iteration are provided by
`@stopcock/async`, not duplicated in the core package.

## Algebra and comparison

| Subpath | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| [`/eq`](/api/algebra) | Lawful equality relations |
| [`/hash`](/api/algebra) | Composable deterministic hashing |
| [`/ord`](/api/algebra) | Total ordering instances |
| `/ordering` | Primitive ordering values and combinators |
| [`/semigroup`](/api/algebra) | Associative combination |
| [`/monoid`](/api/algebra) | Combination with an identity |
| [`/group`](/api/algebra) | Combination with inversion |

## Functions and data transformation

| Subpath | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `/function` | Composition, currying, memoization, predicates, and function utilities |
| `/guard` | Structural guards and refinements |
| `/object` | Immutable object/path operations |
| `/string` | String transforms and predicates |
| `/number` | Numeric predicates, statistics, and safe partials |
| `/math` | Arithmetic pipeline operators |
| `/boolean` | Boolean combinators |
| `/dual` | Build data-first and data-last APIs |
| `/compile` | Portable pipeline planning and explanations |
| [`/optic`](/api/optic) | Lenses, optionals, prisms, traversals, and more |
| `/match` | Exhaustive tagged-value matching |

## Functional models

| Subpath | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `/reader` | Environment-dependent computations |
| `/state-fn` | Pure state transitions |
| `/writer` | Values paired with accumulated output |
| `/recursion` | Stack-safe recursion schemes |

The package export map is generated from one checked-in manifest. CI builds and
imports every runtime and declaration entry from a real packed tarball, so this
catalogue cannot silently advertise a missing module.

---
# N (Number)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/number/

clamp, sum, mean, percentile. Numeric transforms for pipe

## Aggregation

```ts
sum(nums: number[]): number
mean(nums: number[]): Option<number>
median(nums: number[]): Option<number>
variance(nums: number[]): Option<number>
standardDeviation(nums: number[]): Option<number>
min(nums: number[]): Option<number>
max(nums: number[]): Option<number>
minMax(nums: number[]): Option<readonly [number, number]>
```

Every partial aggregate also has an explicit `*OrUndefined` variant. Use the
`*NonEmpty` variants when a readonly non-empty tuple proves a result exists,
and the sample-statistic `*AtLeastTwo` variants when two inputs are required.

## Dual

```ts
percentile(nums: number[], p: number): Option<number>
percentileOrUndefined(nums: number[], p: number): number | undefined
percentileNonEmpty(nums: readonly [number, ...number[]], p: number): number
clamp(value: number, min: number, max: number): number
dotProduct(a: number[], b: number[]): number
```

## Predicates

```ts
isEven(n: number): boolean
isOdd(n: number): boolean
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'
import * as N from '@stopcock/fp/number'
import * as O from '@stopcock/fp/option'

// stats on response times
const times = [120, 95, 200, 88, 150, 300, 110] as const
pipe(N.mean(times), O.getOrElse(() => 0)) // ~151.9
N.medianNonEmpty(times) // 120
N.standardDeviationNonEmpty(times) // ~68.6
N.percentileNonEmpty(times, 95) // 300

// clamp user input
pipe(userAge, N.clamp(0, 150))

// average score, ignoring zeros
pipe(
  scores,
  A.filter((s) => s > 0),
  N.mean,
)

// feature vector similarity
N.dotProduct([1, 0, 1], [0, 1, 1]) // 1
```

---
# Object

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/object/

Safe immutable object, merge, and typed path operations

```ts
import * as Obj from '@stopcock/fp/object'
```

Object operators preserve symbol keys, use own enumerable properties, and
defend write paths against prototype-pollution keys.

## Keys and projections

```ts
Obj.keys(value)
Obj.values(value)
Obj.entries(value)
Obj.pick(value, ['id', 'name'])
Obj.omit(value, ['password'])
Obj.pickBy(value, (_value, key) => key !== 'internal')
Obj.omitBy(value, predicate)
```

`pick`, `omit`, and predicate projections are available in data-first and
pipe-friendly forms.

## Immutable updates

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'

const updated = pipe(
  user,
  Obj.assoc('role', 'admin'),
  Obj.dissoc('temporaryToken'),
  Obj.evolve({
    name: (name) => name.trim(),
  }),
)
```

`mapValues`, `mapKeys`, and `invert` cover whole-object transformations.

## Merge

```ts
Obj.mergeWith(defaults, overrides, (left, right) => right ?? left)

Obj.mergeDeep(defaults, overrides, {
  bias: 'right',
  arrays: 'replace',
})
```

Deep merge options make conflict and array semantics explicit:

- `bias`: choose the left or right value by default.
- `arrays`: `replace`, `concat`, or `merge-index`.
- `onConflict`: resolve non-record values with access to their property path.

Deep merge is cycle-safe for repeated object pairs.

## Typed paths

Paths are readonly key tuples, not dotted strings:

```ts
const cityPath = Obj.pathOf<User>()('profile', 'address', 'city')

Obj.getPath(user, cityPath)            // Option<string>
Obj.getPathOrUndefined(user, cityPath) // string | undefined
Obj.hasPath(user, cityPath)

const moved = Obj.setPath(user, cityPath, 'Manchester')
const upper = Obj.modifyPath(user, cityPath, String.toUpperCase)
const withoutCity = Obj.removePath(user, cityPath)
```

Tuple paths distinguish numeric indices from string keys, reject unsafe write
segments, and infer nested values to a bounded depth.

---
# Optic

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/optic/

Composable immutable focus with lenses, prisms, traversals, and more

```ts
import * as Optic from '@stopcock/fp/optic'
```

The optic module represents immutable reads and updates without hiding
partiality. Its optic kinds are:

| Kind | Focus | Read | Write |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Lens` | exactly one | yes | yes |
| `Optional` | zero or one | `Option` | yes when present |
| `Prism` | one case of a sum | `Option` | yes when matched |
| `Traversal` | zero or more | collect | modify all |
| `Iso` | exactly one | yes | reversible |
| `Getter` | exactly one | yes | no |
| `Fold` | zero or more | collect | no |
| `Setter` | zero or more | no | modify |
| `At` | keyed optional value | `Option` | insert/delete |

## Constructors

```ts
Optic.lens(get, replace)
Optic.optional(preview, replace)
Optic.prism(preview, replace)
Optic.traversal(collect, modify)
Optic.iso(to, from)
Optic.getter(get)
Optic.fold(collect)
Optic.setter(modify)
```

Common focused constructors are provided:

```ts
const name = Optic.prop<User, 'name'>('name')
const first = Optic.index<User>(0)
const admin = Optic.find<User>((user) => user.role === 'admin')
const everyUser = Optic.each<User>()
const adults = Optic.filtered<User>((user) => user.age >= 18)
const preference = Optic.atKey<'theme', Theme>('theme')
const byId = Optic.at<string, User>('user-1')
```

## Read and update

```ts
Optic.view(name, user)
Optic.preview(first, users)       // Option<User>
Optic.collect(adults, users)      // readonly User[]
Optic.set(name, user, 'Ada')
Optic.modify(name, user, (value) => value.toUpperCase())
```

Each operation also has a pipe-friendly form with the optic first:

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'

const updated = pipe(
  user,
  Optic.modify(name, (value) => value.toUpperCase()),
)
```

## Composition

```ts
const city = Optic.compose(
  Optic.prop<User, 'address'>('address'),
  Optic.prop<Address, 'city'>('city'),
)

Optic.view(city, user)
```

Composition preserves the strongest valid optic kind: lens with lens remains
a lens, while partial or multi-focus paths become optional or traversal
optics.

For nested object paths, the fluent builder avoids manual intermediate types:

```ts
const city = Optic.optic<User>()
  .prop('address')
  .prop('city')
  .value
```

`Optic.laws` exposes the standard lens get-set, set-get, and set-set checks for
custom lenses.

---
# O (Option)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/option/

Some and None for missing values. map, flatMap, filter, getOrElse, toResult

```ts
type None = { readonly _tag: 0 }
type Some<A> = { readonly _tag: 1; readonly value: A }
type Option<A> = None | Some<A>
```

Numeric `_tag` for fast branching. `none` is a singleton.

## Constructors

```ts
some<A>(value: A): Option<A>
none: None
fromNullable<A>(value: A | null | undefined): Option<NonNullable<A>>
fromPredicate<A>(value: A, pred: (value: A) => boolean): Option<A>
fromPredicate<A>(pred: (value: A) => boolean): (value: A) => Option<A>
```

Type-guard predicates narrow the `Some` value in both forms.

## Transforms

```ts
map<A, B>(f: (a: A) => B): (o: Option<A>) => Option<B>
flatMap<A, B>(f: (a: A) => Option<B>): (o: Option<A>) => Option<B>
filter<A>(option: Option<A>, pred: (value: A) => boolean): Option<A>
filter<A>(pred: (value: A) => boolean): (option: Option<A>) => Option<A>
tap<A>(f: (a: A) => void): (o: Option<A>) => Option<A>
```

`filter` also preserves type-guard narrowing. Its runtime behavior is unchanged: a matching `Some`
passes through and a failed predicate produces the `none` singleton.

## Extraction

```ts
getOrElse<B>(onNone: () => B): <A>(o: Option<A>) => A | B
getOrThrow<A>(option: Option<A>, onNone?: () => unknown): A
match<A, B, C>({ none: () => B, some: (a: A) => C }): (o: Option<A>) => B | C
toNullable<A>(o: Option<A>): A | null
toUndefined<A>(o: Option<A>): A | undefined
toResult<E>(onNone: () => E): <A>(o: Option<A>) => Result<A, E>
```

## Guards

```ts
isSome<A>(o: Option<A>): o is Some<A>
isNone<A>(o: Option<A>): o is None
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as O from '@stopcock/fp/option'

// safe env variable with validation
const port = pipe(
  O.fromNullable(process.env.PORT),
  O.map((s) => parseInt(s, 10)),
  O.filter((n) => n > 0 && n < 65536),
  O.getOrElse(() => 3000),
)

const directPort = O.fromPredicate(3000, (port) => port > 0 && port < 65536)

// chain nullable lookups
pipe(
  O.fromNullable(user.address),
  O.flatMap((a) => O.fromNullable(a.zip)),
  O.match({
    none: () => 'no zip',
    some: (zip) => zip,
  }),
)

// convert to Result for error context
pipe(
  O.fromNullable(headers.authorization),
  O.toResult(() => 'missing auth header'),
)
```

---
# R (Result)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/result/

Fail-fast recoverable errors, refinement, traversal, and optional decoding

```ts
type Err<E> = { readonly _tag: 0; readonly error: E }
type Ok<A> = { readonly _tag: 1; readonly value: A }
type Result<A, E> = Ok<A> | Err<E>
```

## Constructors

```ts
ok<A>(value: A): Result<A, never>
err<E>(error: E): Result<never, E>
tryCatch<A>(thunk: () => A): Result<A, unknown>
fromNullable<E>(onNullish: () => E): <A>(value: A | null | undefined) => Result<NonNullable<A>, E>
fromPredicate<A, E>(value: A, predicate: (value: A) => boolean, onFalse: (value: A) => E): Result<A, E>
fromPredicate<A, E>(predicate: (value: A) => boolean, onFalse: (value: A) => E): (value: A) => Result<A, E>
```

`tryCatch` wraps a function that might throw. Error comes back as `unknown`, narrow it yourself.
When `predicate` is a type guard, `fromPredicate` narrows the successful value. `onFalse` receives
the rejected value and runs only when the predicate fails.

## Transforms

```ts
map<A, B>(f: (a: A) => B): <E>(r: Result<A, E>) => Result<B, E>
mapErr<E, F>(f: (e: E) => F): <A>(r: Result<A, E>) => Result<A, F>
flatMap<A, B, E2>(f: (a: A) => Result<B, E2>): <E>(r: Result<A, E>) => Result<B, E | E2>
filterOrElse<A, E, E2>(result: Result<A, E>, predicate: (value: A) => boolean, onFalse: (value: A) => E2): Result<A, E | E2>
filterOrElse<A, E2>(predicate: (value: A) => boolean, onFalse: (value: A) => E2): <E>(result: Result<A, E>) => Result<A, E | E2>
tap<A>(f: (a: A) => void): <E>(r: Result<A, E>) => Result<A, E>
tapErr<E>(f: (e: E) => void): <A>(r: Result<A, E>) => Result<A, E>
```

`filterOrElse` also narrows with type guards. Existing errors pass through unchanged; neither the
predicate nor `onFalse` runs for them.

## Composition

```ts
all<T extends readonly Result<unknown, unknown>[]>(results: T): Result<ValuesOf<T>, ErrorsOf<T>>
sequence: typeof all

traverse<A, B, E>(values: readonly A[], decode: (value: A) => Result<B, E>): Result<B[], E>
traverse<A, B, E>(decode: (value: A) => Result<B, E>): (values: readonly A[]) => Result<B[], E>

optional<A, B, E>(value: A | undefined, decode: (value: A) => Result<B, E>): Result<B | undefined, E>
nullable<A, B, E>(value: A | null, decode: (value: A) => Result<B, E>): Result<B | null, E>
```

`all` and its exact alias `sequence` keep tuple types and return the first error from left to right.
`traverse` stops calling the decoder after its first error. Empty inputs return `ok([])`.

`optional` skips decoding only for `undefined`; `nullable` skips only for `null`. The other sentinel
is passed to the decoder like any other value. Both also support data-last calls:
`R.optional(decode)(value)` and `R.nullable(decode)(value)`.

## Extraction

```ts
getOrElse<B>(onErr: () => B): <A, E>(r: Result<A, E>) => A | B
match<A, E, B, C>({ err: (e: E) => B, ok: (a: A) => C }): (r: Result<A, E>) => B | C
toOption<A, E>(r: Result<A, E>): Option<A>
```

## Guards

```ts
isOk<A, E>(r: Result<A, E>): r is Ok<A>
isErr<A, E>(r: Result<A, E>): r is Err<E>
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as G from '@stopcock/fp/guard'
import * as R from '@stopcock/fp/result'

// parse JSON safely
const data = pipe(
  R.tryCatch(() => JSON.parse(rawBody)),
  R.map((body: { items: string[] }) => body.items),
  R.getOrElse((): string[] => []),
)

// narrow an unknown request body
const body = R.fromPredicate(rawBody, G.isPlainObject, () => 'expected an object')

// decode optional and nullable request fields without conflating their sentinels
const limit = R.optional(request.limit, decodePositiveInteger)
const displayName = R.nullable(request.displayName, decodeNonBlankString)

// chain validations
pipe(
  R.ok(formData),
  R.flatMap((d) => (d.name ? R.ok(d) : R.err('name required'))),
  R.flatMap((d) => (d.email ? R.ok(d) : R.err('email required'))),
  R.match({
    err: (error) => ({ success: false as const, error }),
    ok: (data) => ({ success: true as const, data }),
  }),
)

// log errors without changing the pipeline
pipe(
  R.tryCatch(() => connectToDb()),
  R.tapErr((e) => console.error('db connection failed:', e)),
  R.getOrElse(() => fallbackDb),
)
```

---
# Schema interop

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/schema/

Standard Schema V1 adapters without a second validation framework

```ts
import * as Schema from '@stopcock/fp/schema'
```

The schema module implements the
[Standard Schema V1](https://standardschema.dev/) interface. It lets
`@stopcock/fp` produce and consume validators shared with schema libraries,
forms, RPC frameworks, and other Standard Schema-aware tools without growing a
competing schema language.

## Create a schema

```ts
const positive = Schema.fromPredicate(
  (value: unknown): value is number =>
    typeof value === 'number' && value > 0,
  () => Schema.issue('Expected a positive number'),
)
```

For decoders and transformations, use `make`:

```ts
import { err, ok } from '@stopcock/fp'

const integerFromString = Schema.make((value) => {
  if (typeof value !== 'string') return err('Expected a string')
  const parsed = Number(value)
  return Number.isInteger(parsed)
    ? ok(parsed)
    : err(Schema.issue('Expected an integer'))
})
```

A decoder may return a `Result` or a promise of a `Result`. String errors,
individual issues, and issue arrays are normalized to Standard Schema issues.

## Consume any Standard Schema

```ts
const result = Schema.validateSync(input, schema)
// Result<Output, readonly Issue[]>

const asyncResult = await Schema.validate(input, schema)
// Promise<Result<Output, readonly Issue[]>>
```

`validateSync` throws a `TypeError` if the validator is asynchronous.
`validate` accepts either kind.

```ts
Schema.isStandardSchema(value)
Schema.issues(error)
Schema.issue(message, path)
```

## Combinators

```ts
const labelled = Schema.map(positive, (value) => `positive:${value}`)
const maybePositive = Schema.optional(positive)
const nullablePositive = Schema.nullable(positive)
```

These combinators preserve a synchronous underlying validator. Wrapping a sync
schema never introduces a promise.

---
# S (String)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/string/

trim, split, replace, startsWith, slice. String transforms for pipe

## Non-dual

```ts
trim(s: string): string
trimStart(s: string): string
trimEnd(s: string): string
toLowerCase(s: string): string
toUpperCase(s: string): string
isEmpty(s: string): boolean
length(s: string): number
```

## Dual

```ts
startsWith(s: string, search: string): boolean
endsWith(s: string, search: string): boolean
includes(s: string, search: string): boolean
split(s: string, sep: string): string[]
repeat(s: string, n: number): string
slice(s: string, start: number, end: number): string
replaceAll(s: string, search: string, replacement: string): string
```

## Examples

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as S from '@stopcock/fp/string'

// slug from title
pipe('  Hello World!  ', S.trim, S.toLowerCase, S.replaceAll(' ', '-'), S.replaceAll('!', ''))
// 'hello-world'

// parse CSV header
pipe('name,email,role', S.split(','))
// ['name', 'email', 'role']

// check file extension
pipe('report.pdf', S.endsWith('.pdf')) // true

// template
pipe('Hello, NAME!', S.replaceAll('NAME', user.name))

// truncate
const preview = pipe(description, S.slice(0, 100))
```

# V (Validation)

Source: https://stopcock.dev/api/validation/

Accumulate independent validation errors while staying compatible with Result

Validation is for independent checks where callers need every error in one pass. It uses the same
runtime representation as `Result`, but its error side is guaranteed to be non-empty.

```ts
type NonEmptyArray<E> = readonly [E, ...E[]]
type Validation<A, E> = Result<A, NonEmptyArray<E>>
```

## Constructors

```ts
valid<A>(value: A): Validation<A, never>
invalid<E>(error: E): Validation<never, E>
fromResult<A, E>(result: Result<A, E>): Validation<A, E>

fromPredicate<A, E>(
  value: A,
  predicate: (value: A) => boolean,
  onFalse: (value: A) => E,
): Validation<A, E>

fromPredicate<A, E>(
  predicate: (value: A) => boolean,
  onFalse: (value: A) => E,
): (value: A) => Validation<A, E>
```

`invalid(error)` stores one error in a `NonEmptyArray`. `fromResult` preserves a success and wraps
one Result error. Type-guard predicates narrow the successful value, and `onFalse` is lazy.

## Accumulation

```ts
all<T extends readonly Validation<unknown, unknown>[]>(
  validations: T,
): Validation<ValuesOf<T>, ErrorsOf<T>>

traverse<A, B, E>(
  values: readonly A[],
  validate: (value: A) => Validation<B, E>,
): Validation<B[], E>

traverse<A, B, E>(
  validate: (value: A) => Validation<B, E>,
): (values: readonly A[]) => Validation<B[], E>
```

`all` preserves heterogeneous tuple types and flattens every validation error in stable input order.
`traverse` calls the validator for every input, even after failures. Empty inputs return `valid([])`.

```ts
import * as R from '@stopcock/fp/result'
import * as V from '@stopcock/fp/validation'

type FieldError = { field: string; message: string }

const signup = V.all([
  V.fromPredicate(
    email,
    (value) => value.includes('@'),
    () => ({
      field: 'email',
      message: 'invalid email',
    }),
  ),
  V.fromPredicate(
    password,
    (value) => value.length >= 8,
    () => ({
      field: 'password',
      message: 'too short',
    }),
  ),
] as const)

R.match({
  err: (errors) => showErrors(errors),
  ok: ([validEmail, validPassword]) => submit(validEmail, validPassword),
})(signup)
```

## Result compatibility

Validation is structurally a Result, so use existing Result transforms and extraction:

```ts
R.map(normalize)(validation)
R.match({ err: showErrors, ok: submit })(validation)
R.getOrElse(() => fallback)(validation)
```

There is deliberately no `flatMap` in the validation module. Dependent
sequential checks are fail-fast and belong in `R.flatMap`; use Validation only
to accumulate checks that can all run independently.

---
# How portable pipeline fusion works

Source: https://stopcock.dev/blog/how-pipe-fuses-your-loops/


> Updated for `@stopcock/fp` 2.0. The old runtime-JIT design was removed.

Ordinary array chains allocate intermediate arrays:

```ts
const result = users
  .filter((user) => user.active)
  .map((user) => user.name)
  .slice(0, 10)
```

Stopcock operators carry small internal operation tags:

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'

const result = pipe(
  users,
  A.filter((user) => user.active),
  A.map((user) => user.name),
  A.take(10),
)
```

The planner recognizes compatible tagged segments and dispatches to checked-in,
hand-shaped loop templates. A filter/map/take segment behaves roughly like:

```ts
const output = []
for (let index = 0; index < users.length; index++) {
  const user = users[index]
  if (!user.active) continue
  output.push(user.name)
  if (output.length === 10) break
}
```

There is no `eval`, `new Function`, function-source parsing, or dynamically
loaded JIT chunk in the public runtime graph. This keeps the same code valid
under strict CSP and across Node, Bun, Deno, browsers, workers, and edge
runtimes.

## Plan once for repeated work

For a hot pipeline used with many inputs, compile its shape once:

```ts
import { compile, explain } from '@stopcock/fp'

const activeNames = compile(
  A.filter((user: User) => user.active),
  A.map((user) => user.name),
  A.take(10),
)

activeNames(firstPage)
activeNames(secondPage)

console.log(
  explain(
    A.filter((user: User) => user.active),
    A.map((user) => user.name),
    A.take(10),
  ),
)
```

`compile` keeps normal callback semantics. `compilePure` is an explicit promise
that callbacks are pure and may enable additional rewrites. Purity is never
silently guessed from `Function#toString`.

## Boundaries

Item-by-item transforms such as map, filter, reject, filter-map, take, and drop
can share a streaming segment. Whole-input operations such as sorting,
reversing, grouping, and global deduplication form materialization boundaries.
Terminals such as reduce, count, sum, and short-circuit searches can finish a
segment without another intermediate collection.

Specialized optimizations are semantic, not magical. For example, a sorted
top-k request can select and sort only the required prefix when its ordering
contract allows that rewrite.

## Build-time lowering

`@stopcock/fp-compiler` is an optional build plugin for Vite/Rollup-compatible
hosts. It recognizes ordinary imports from `@stopcock/fp` and
`@stopcock/fp/array`, lowers supported call sites to direct loops, and emits
diagnostics for transformed or rejected shapes. It is a development dependency;
applications do not import it at runtime.

## When fusion helps

Measure your workload. Fusion is most useful for large inputs, early exit,
multiple compatible stages, and repeated hot paths. For a short collection or
a single native operation, clarity usually matters more than forcing a
compiled plan.

The benchmark suite measures source and packed-dist lanes on the real runtime
engine. Release gates compare the build compiler with a frozen loop emitter on
Linux x64 and macOS arm64 and reject correctness mismatches as well as
performance regressions.

---
# Zustand without the spread

Source: https://stopcock.dev/blog/zustand-without-the-spread/


Nested immutable updates quickly become a wall of spread operators:

```ts
setCity: (city) =>
  set((state) => ({
    ...state,
    user: {
      ...state.user,
      address: {
        ...state.user.address,
        city,
      },
    },
  }))
```

An optic packages the read and immutable-update path as a reusable value.

```ts
import * as Optic from '@stopcock/fp/optic'

const city = Optic.optic<State>()
  .prop('user')
  .prop('address')
  .prop('city')
  .value
```

The Zustand action becomes:

```ts
setCity: (value) =>
  set((state) => Optic.set(city, state, value))
```

## A complete store

```ts
import { create } from 'zustand'
import * as Optic from '@stopcock/fp/optic'

const city = Optic.optic<State>().prop('user').prop('address').prop('city').value
const theme = Optic.optic<State>().prop('ui').prop('theme').value
const sidebar = Optic.optic<State>().prop('ui').prop('sidebarOpen').value
const discount = Optic.optic<State>().prop('cart').prop('discount').value

const useStore = create<State & Actions>((set) => ({
  user: {
    name: 'Alice',
    address: {
      street: '123 Main St',
      city: 'Portland',
      postcode: '97201',
    },
  },
  cart: { items: [], discount: null },
  ui: { sidebarOpen: false, theme: 'light' },

  setCity: (value) => set((state) => Optic.set(city, state, value)),
  setTheme: (value) => set((state) => Optic.set(theme, state, value)),
  applyDiscount: (value) => set((state) => Optic.set(discount, state, value)),
  toggleSidebar: () =>
    set((state) => Optic.modify(sidebar, state, (open) => !open)),
}))
```

The optic is defined once, inferred from `State`, and independently testable.

## Conditional array updates

Traversals focus on zero or more values:

```ts
const outOfStock = Optic.filtered<CartItem>((item) => item.stock === 0)

const updatedItems = Optic.modify(
  outOfStock,
  items,
  (item) => ({ ...item, disabled: true }),
)
```

Compose the traversal with a lens to update items directly inside state:

```ts
const cartItems = Optic.optic<State>().prop('cart').prop('items').value
const unavailableItems = Optic.compose(cartItems, outOfStock)

const markOutOfStock = () =>
  set((state) =>
    Optic.modify(
      unavailableItems,
      state,
      (item) => ({ ...item, disabled: true }),
    ),
  )
```

## Partial focus

`index` and `find` produce `Optional` optics. Reads return `Option`; writes
leave the source unchanged when no focus exists.

```ts
const selected = Optic.find<CartItem>((item) => item.id === selectedId)
const current = Optic.preview(selected, items)
const renamed = Optic.modify(selected, items, (item) => ({
  ...item,
  name: item.name.trim(),
}))
```

## When to use optics

Flat state rarely needs them. Optics pay off when paths are nested, shared by
several actions, partial, or multi-focus. The 2.0 module also includes prisms,
isomorphisms, getters, folds, setters, keyed `At` optics, composition, and lens
law checks.

---
# Fusion

Source: https://stopcock.dev/concepts/fusion/

How pipe fuses array operations

When you chain streaming [array operations](/api/array) in `pipe`, they fuse into a single loop.

Without fusion:

```text
data [100K] -> filter -> [50K] -> map -> [50K] -> take(10) -> [10]
```

Three passes. Two throwaway arrays.

With fusion:

```text
data [100K] -> fused(filter + map + take) -> [10]
```

One pass. `take(10)` breaks the loop after 10 results.

## What fuses

| Operation                                                            | Position                  | Notes                                                                                         |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `map`, `filter`, `flatMap`, `take`, `drop`, `takeWhile`, `dropWhile` | streaming-fused           | inlined into the loop; `take` and `takeWhile` can stop early                                  |
| `reduce`, `find`, `every`, `some`, `count`                           | terminal folds/predicates | finish the fused pass and return a scalar or found value                                      |
| `head`, `last`, `length`, `join`, `sum`, `min`, `max`                | accessor terminals        | end the chain with a scalar or aggregate result                                               |
| `sort`, `sortBy`, `reverse`, `groupBy`, `uniq`                       | materialization boundary  | need a completed array before the next step                                                   |
| `sortBy -> take(k)`, `sort -> take(k)` under `compilePure`           | opt-in top-k rewrite      | uses a bounded, stable top-k path when the caller explicitly promises callback purity          |

Operations that need the whole array break the streaming chain. Everything before them gets fused and runs first, then the materializing op runs on that result:

```ts
pipe(
  data,
  A.filter((x) => x > 3), // segment 1
  A.map((x) => x * 2),
  A.sortBy((a, b) => a - b), // runs on the materialized array
  A.take(3), // exact pipe semantics: take runs after the complete sort
)
```

`compilePure(A.sortBy(compare), A.take(k))` may replace that exact pair with
the bounded top-k rewrite. Ordinary `pipe` and `compile` keep exact callback
semantics and complete the sort. Import `explainPure` from
`@stopcock/fp/compile` to inspect the applied rewrite. Inserting another
operation between sort and take prevents the rewrite.

## Mechanics

Functions created by `dual()` carry compact internal operation and binding
metadata. `pipe` reads those tags and dispatches consecutive compatible
operations to checked-in portable loop templates or a closure-based generic
lowering. Early-exit operations stop the shared loop as soon as their contract
allows. Untagged user functions pass through as ordinary opaque pipeline
steps.

There is no runtime source generation. If nothing is fuseable, `pipe` applies
functions one after another as expected.

See [Benchmarks](/performance/benchmarks) for how fusion compares to lodash, ramda, and native JS.

---
# Option and Result

Source: https://stopcock.dev/concepts/option-result/

Explicit absence and recoverable failure

Use `Option<A>` when a value may be absent. Use `Result<A, E>` when a
recoverable operation can explain why it failed. Both make the unhappy path
part of the type instead of encoding it as `null`, an exception, or a
success-flag convention.

```ts
import * as O from '@stopcock/fp/option'
import * as R from '@stopcock/fp/result'
```

## Option

```ts
type None = { readonly _tag: 0 }
type Some<A> = { readonly _tag: 1; readonly value: A }
type Option<A> = None | Some<A>
```

Create options at nullable and predicate boundaries:

```ts
const portText = O.fromNullable(process.env.PORT)
const positive = O.fromPredicate(3, (value) => value > 0)
```

Then transform without repeatedly branching:

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'

const port = pipe(
  portText,
  O.map(Number),
  O.filter((value) => Number.isInteger(value) && value > 0),
  O.getOrElse(() => 3000),
)
```

`mapNullable`, `flatMap`, `filter`, `zip`, `all`, `struct`, and `traverse`
cover the common composition shapes. Partial extraction is explicit:

```ts
const label = O.match({
  none: () => 'not configured',
  some: (value) => `port ${value}`,
})(portText)
```

`none` is a frozen singleton. The representation uses numeric tags: `0` is
`None`, `1` is `Some`.

## Result

```ts
type Err<E> = { readonly _tag: 0; readonly error: E }
type Ok<A> = { readonly _tag: 1; readonly value: A }
type Result<A, E> = Ok<A> | Err<E>
```

Translate throwing and nullable APIs at the boundary:

```ts
type ParseError = {
  readonly type: 'InvalidJson'
  readonly cause: unknown
}

const parsed = R.tryCatch(
  () => JSON.parse(input) as unknown,
  (cause): ParseError => ({ type: 'InvalidJson', cause }),
)

const token = R.fromNullable(() => 'Missing token')(
  headers.authorization,
)
```

`map` transforms success. `mapErr` transforms failure. `flatMap` sequences
dependent work and keeps the union of possible error types.

```ts
const response = pipe(
  parsed,
  R.flatMap(decodeRequest),
  R.flatMap(authorizeRequest),
  R.match({
    err: (error) => ({ status: 400, error }),
    ok: (value) => ({ status: 200, value }),
  }),
)
```

`all`, `struct`, and `traverse` are fail-fast and preserve tuple/object types.
Use [`Validation`](/api/validation) when independent checks must all run and
accumulate errors.

## Conversion

```ts
O.toResult(() => 'missing')(option)
R.toOption(result) // intentionally discards the error
O.transpose(optionOfResult)
```

Asynchronous failure belongs in `Task` from `@stopcock/async`. Keeping
`Option`, `Result`, and `Task` separate makes evaluation and cancellation
semantics visible.

---
# Cookbook

Source: https://stopcock.dev/cookbook/

Practical @stopcock/fp 2.0 recipes

## Transform a collection

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'

const cards = pipe(
  products,
  A.filter((product) => product.inStock),
  A.map((product) => ({
    id: product.id,
    label: product.name,
    price: product.price,
  })),
  A.take(20),
)
```

Use direct form when it reads more naturally:

```ts
const cards = A.map(products, toCard)
```

## Compile a repeated hot path

```ts
import { compile, explain } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'

const activeIds = compile(
  A.filter((user: User) => user.active),
  A.map((user) => user.id),
  A.take(100),
)

activeIds(firstBatch)
activeIds(secondBatch)
console.log(explain(A.filter((user: User) => user.active), A.map((user) => user.id)))
```

Use `compilePure` only when every callback is pure and the extra rewrite
freedom is valid for your code.

## Read optional configuration

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as O from '@stopcock/fp/option'

const port = pipe(
  O.fromNullable(process.env.PORT),
  O.map(Number),
  O.filter((value) => Number.isSafeInteger(value) && value > 0 && value < 65_536),
  O.getOrElse(() => 3000),
)
```

## Decode fail-fast input

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as G from '@stopcock/fp/guard'
import * as R from '@stopcock/fp/result'

type DecodeError =
  | { readonly type: 'InvalidJson'; readonly cause: unknown }
  | { readonly type: 'ExpectedObject' }

const decodeBody = (text: string) =>
  pipe(
    R.tryCatch(
      () => JSON.parse(text) as unknown,
      (cause): DecodeError => ({ type: 'InvalidJson', cause }),
    ),
    R.filterOrElse(
      G.isPlainObject,
      (): DecodeError => ({ type: 'ExpectedObject' }),
    ),
  )
```

## Accumulate independent field errors

```ts
import * as V from '@stopcock/fp/validation'

type FieldError = {
  readonly field: string
  readonly message: string
}

const signup = V.all([
  V.fromPredicate(
    email,
    (value) => value.includes('@'),
    (): FieldError => ({ field: 'email', message: 'invalid email' }),
  ),
  V.fromPredicate(
    password,
    (value) => value.length >= 12,
    (): FieldError => ({ field: 'password', message: 'too short' }),
  ),
] as const)
```

Use `Result.flatMap` for checks that depend on earlier values. Use Validation
only when every check can run independently.

## Validate through Standard Schema

```ts
import * as Schema from '@stopcock/fp/schema'

const userId = Schema.fromPredicate(
  (value: unknown): value is string =>
    typeof value === 'string' && value.length > 0,
  () => Schema.issue('Expected a user id', ['id']),
)

const decoded = Schema.validateSync(input, userId)
```

The same consumer accepts a Standard Schema produced by another library.

## Stream a large or infinite sequence

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as Iter from '@stopcock/fp/iter'

const firstTenEvenSquares = pipe(
  Iter.range(1, Infinity),
  Iter.filter((value) => value % 2 === 0),
  Iter.map((value) => value * value),
  Iter.take(10),
  Iter.toArray,
)
```

For asynchronous sources, use `AsyncIter` from `@stopcock/async`.

## Update nested data immutably

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as Optic from '@stopcock/fp/optic'

const city = Optic.optic<User>()
  .prop('profile')
  .prop('address')
  .prop('city')
  .value

const moved = pipe(
  user,
  Optic.set(city, 'Manchester'),
)
```

## Group and aggregate records

```ts
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'

const revenueByRegion = A.groupMapReduce(
  orders,
  (order) => order.region,
  (order) => order.total,
  (left, right) => left + right,
)
```

`groupMapReduce`, `countBy`, `partitionMap`, binary search, combinations, and
explicit `mapInto`/`filterInto` operations live in the array subpath.

## Match tagged domain values

```ts
import * as Match from '@stopcock/fp/match'

type Payment =
  | { readonly type: 'Pending'; readonly id: string }
  | { readonly type: 'Paid'; readonly id: string; readonly receipt: string }
  | { readonly type: 'Failed'; readonly id: string; readonly reason: string }

const label = (payment: Payment) =>
  Match.discriminant('type', payment, {
    Pending: (value) => `Pending ${value.id}`,
    Paid: (value) => `Receipt ${value.receipt}`,
    Failed: (value) => `Failed: ${value.reason}`,
  })
```

The handler object must cover every tag. Use the pattern module for structural
patterns once simple tagged dispatch is no longer enough.

---
# Getting Started

Source: https://stopcock.dev/getting-started/

Install stopcock and build your first pipe with fusion, Option, and Result

```bash
bun add @stopcock/fp
```

```ts
import { flow, pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'
import * as O from '@stopcock/fp/option'
import * as R from '@stopcock/fp/result'
```

## pipe

Pass a value through functions, left to right. If you chain array operations, they get fused into single loops automatically.

```ts
type User = { name: string; active: boolean; score: number }

const leaderboard = pipe(
  users,
  A.filter((u: User) => u.active && u.score > 0),
  A.sortBy((a: User, b: User) => b.score - a.score),
  A.take(10),
  A.map((u: User) => u.name),
)
```

Portable tagged operators can be planned into a single loop. `take(10)`
terminates early, so work stops after ten matching results.

## flow

Same as `pipe` but gives you a reusable function instead of running straight away.

```ts
const activeNames = flow(
  A.filter((u: User) => u.active),
  A.map((u: User) => u.name),
)

activeNames(usersA)
activeNames(usersB)
```

## Fusion

`pipe` recognizes tagged array operations and uses checked-in portable loop
templates. `take` and short-circuiting terminals can stop before the input is
exhausted.

```ts
const big = Array.from({ length: 1_000_000 }, (_, i) => i)

// visits ~70 items, allocates nothing intermediate
pipe(
  big,
  A.filter((x) => x % 7 === 0),
  A.map((x) => x * 2),
  A.take(10),
)
```

Operations that need the whole array (`sort`, `groupBy`, `uniq`) break the fusion chain. See [Fusion](/concepts/fusion) for the full picture.

## Dual signatures

Every function works both ways:

```ts
A.take(users, 5) // data-first
pipe(users, A.take(5)) // data-last
```

## Option and Result

```ts
pipe(
  O.fromNullable(user.email),
  O.map((e) => e.split('@')[1]),
  O.getOrElse(() => 'unknown'),
)

pipe(
  R.tryCatch(() => JSON.parse(input)),
  R.map((obj: { value: number }) => obj.value),
  R.getOrElse(() => null),
)
```

See [Option & Result](/concepts/option-result) for the full API, or try the [Cookbook](/cookbook) for more patterns.

---
# A TypeScript toolkit

Source: https://stopcock.dev/

Fast, composable TypeScript. FP primitives, dates, async tasks, image processing.

A focused set of TypeScript packages that play nicely together. Pipeable
utilities sit alongside persistent collections, parsing, pattern matching,
async tasks, HTTP, state, diffing, numerical tools, graphics, and dedicated
testing and migration tooling.

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import * as A from '@stopcock/fp/array'

const top10 = pipe(
  users,
  A.filter((u) => u.active),
  A.map((u) => ({ name: u.name, score: u.score })),
  A.take(10),
)
```

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import { now, add, format } from '@stopcock/date'

const nextWeek = pipe(now(), add(7, 'day'), format('YYYY-MM-DD'))
```

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import { fromPromise, map, flatMap, retry, timeout, run } from '@stopcock/async'

const fetchUser = pipe(
  fromPromise(() => fetch('/api/user')),
  flatMap((res) => fromPromise(() => res.json())),
  map((data) => data.name),
  retry({ attempts: 3 }),
  timeout(5000),
)

const name = await run(fetchUser)
```

```ts
import { diff, apply, invert } from '@stopcock/diff'

const before = { user: 'Tom', scores: [10, 20] }
const after = { user: 'Tom', scores: [10, 20, 30] }
const patch = diff(before, after)
const restored = apply(after, invert(patch))
```

```ts
import { create, history } from '@stopcock/state'

const store = create({ count: 0, name: 'Tom' })
store.subscribe(
  (s) => s.count,
  (next) => console.log(next),
)
store.set((s) => s.count, 1)
```

```ts
import { pipe } from '@stopcock/fp'
import { fromRGBA, resize, sharpen, contrast } from '@stopcock/img'

const thumbnail = (data: Uint8ClampedArray, w: number, h: number) =>
  pipe(fromRGBA(data, w, h), resize(200, 200), sharpen, contrast(30))
```

---

## Array pipelines fuse automatically

`pipe` detects chainable array operations and fuses them into a single loop. `take(10)` bails after 10 hits. On a million-element array, that's dozens of items touched instead of three full passes.


---

```bash
bun add @stopcock/fp
```
